abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel semantic graph traversal paradigm for multimedia retrieval that fundamentally rethinks the traditional vector-based similarity computation approach. Existing methods predominantly rely on embedding spaces where semantic relationships are implicitly encoded, often failing to capture complex multimedia data correlations across heterogeneous modalities. We propose the Semantic Relationship Propagation Network (SRPN), a theoretical framework that models multimedia objects as nodes in a dynamically constructed knowledge graph, where edges represent semantic dependencies learned through cross-modal attention mechanisms. The framework establishes a new theoretical foundation for retrieval by formalizing the problem as graph propagation with adaptive edge weights that evolve based on query context. Our analysis demonstrates that SRPN achieves superior performance by enabling transitive semantic inference that traditional methods cannot support. Experimental evaluation on benchmark datasets including MS COCO and Flicker30K validates the theoretical claims, showing significant improvements in retrieval accuracy and semantic consistency. The proposed paradigm opens new research directions for multimedia indexing by shifting from static embedding spaces to dynamic semantic networks, fundamentally transforming how relevance is computed in multimedia databases.

This paper presents an enhanced theoretical framework for adaptive bitrate streaming optimization in multimedia systems, addressing the fundamental limitations of existing quality-of-experience (QoE) models. Traditional approaches treat video quality, buffering time, and switching frequency as independent factors, leading to suboptimal streaming decisions in dynamic network environments. We propose a unified QoE maximization theory that models the complex interdependencies among these metrics through a multi-objective optimization framework with learned trade-off parameters. The theoretical contribution includes formal proofs demonstrating that our approach achieves Pareto-optimal streaming decisions under stochastic network conditions. We introduce a novel utility function that captures user perception characteristics based on Weber-Fechner law, providing deeper theoretical grounding for QoE modeling. Simulation results across diverse network scenarios show that our framework improves average QoE scores by 23% compared to state-of-the-art methods while maintaining computational tractability. This work significantly advances multimedia networking theory by providing rigorous mathematical foundations for adaptive streaming decision-making that can be directly applied to practical systems.

This paper presents EdgeMedia, a groundbreaking edge-centric multimedia processing architecture that fundamentally reimagines where and how multimedia data is processed in distributed systems. Conventional approaches centralize multimedia analysis in cloud datacenters, creating inherent limitations in latency, bandwidth, and privacy that cannot be resolved through incremental optimization. EdgeMedia introduces a hierarchical fog computing framework where edge devices perform real-time semantic analysis, only transmitting high-level feature abstractions to central servers. The system architecture comprises three novel components: a lightweight neural inference engine optimized for resource-constrained edge devices, a dynamic feature fusion protocol that maintains semantic consistency across distributed processing nodes, and a context-aware task scheduling mechanism that intelligently partitions workloads based on device capabilities and network conditions. We implement EdgeMedia as a complete system and evaluate its performance across video surveillance and augmented reality applications. Results demonstrate end-to-end latency reductions of 67% compared to cloud-only approaches while preserving 94% of analytical accuracy. This architecture establishes a new paradigm for multimedia applications by enabling intelligent processing at the network edge.

This paper introduces DeepIndex, an advanced multimedia indexing system that significantly improves upon existing content-based retrieval architectures through innovative feature fusion and query optimization mechanisms. While current systems achieve acceptable performance on single-modality queries, they struggle with complex cross-modal search scenarios that increasingly dominate modern applications. DeepIndex addresses these limitations through three key system innovations: a hierarchical feature embedding module that jointly optimizes visual, audio, and textual representations in a unified space; an adaptive inverted index structure that dynamically adjusts posting list ordering based on query characteristics; and a learned query expansion technique that leverages attention-weighted pseudo-relevance feedback. The system architecture incorporates efficient batching strategies and GPU-accelerated similarity computation to handle large-scale multimedia databases with billions of items. Extensive experiments conducted on Vimeo-90K and AudioSet demonstrate that DeepIndex achieves a 31% improvement in mean average precision for cross-modal retrieval tasks while maintaining sub-second query response times for datasets containing 10 million multimedia items. This work provides a practical solution for building scalable multimedia databases with enhanced retrieval capabilities.
